plot_extraction.response_text:
Jessamine Stacy, a country woman forced to live in the city after losing her family home, becomes an unpaid servant in her brother John’s household. Overworked, neglected, and desperately homesick, she grows thin and unhappy under her demanding sister-in-law.

When the usual vegetable seller breaks his leg, his nephew, Andrew Bell, temporarily takes over his route. He notices Jessamine’s longing for the countryside and begins bringing her wildflowers. After learning that she is unmarried and merely treated like a servant in her brother’s home, Andrew befriends her and invites her on a country drive to Cloverside Farm. There, welcomed by his aunt and surrounded by fields, woods, flowers, and animals, Jessamine briefly regains her happiness and vitality.

Andrew realizes he loves her and wants to give her the affectionate country home she craves. After his uncle resumes the vegetable route, Andrew is absent during the harvest. When he returns, he learns that John has failed in business and that Jessamine is expected to move west with the family. Andrew immediately asks her to marry him and live at Cloverside Farm. Overwhelmed that someone truly cares for her, Jessamine accepts. Despite her sister-in-law’s resentment, Andrew marries Jessamine and takes her back to the countryside, where she finds lasting love and happiness.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a warm, sentimental, old-fashioned romantic style, shaped like a compact domestic fairy tale. Its emotional world is morally clear: kindness, rural life and affectionate companionship are restorative, while the city household represents confinement, neglect and exploitation. The narrative moves steadily from deprivation to rescue, giving the story an optimistic, reassuring arc rather than pursuing ambiguity or psychological complexity.

The narration is in the third person, with a gently omniscient perspective that moves chiefly between Jessamine and Andrew Bell. Jessamine’s homesickness and exhaustion are presented through free indirect description and sensuous memories, while Andrew’s feelings are frequently disclosed in candid interior monologues. His thoughts—such as comparing Jessamine to a caged lark or wondering why he cannot see her at his farm every evening—make his intentions transparent and remove romantic suspense in favour of emotional security. The narrator is sympathetic and unobtrusively judgmental, clearly aligning the reader with Jessamine and Andrew against the selfish Mrs. John and inattentive brother.

The prose is accessible, graceful and moderately descriptive. Sentences are generally clear and conventional, with longer, flowing constructions used for pastoral description and shorter sentences used to advance action. The vocabulary is domestic and concrete, enriched by lyrical nature imagery: honeysuckle, sweet-brier roses, clover, ferns, buttercups, maples, blue skies and purple hills. Colour, fragrance, light and spaciousness recur throughout. These details establish a strong opposition between the “hot and stifling” city kitchen and the open, fertile countryside, where Jessamine can once again “live and breathe.” Nature functions symbolically as well as decoratively: flowers chart her emotional revival, and the return of roses to her cheeks mirrors the blossoms Andrew brings her.

Dialogue occupies a large proportion of the story and is used to develop intimacy quickly. Jessamine speaks politely, hesitantly and with emotional openness, while Andrew’s speech is hearty, direct and colloquial. Expressions such as “for a spell,” “posies,” “I reckon,” and “You don’t say” give him a genial rural voice. His figurative language is homely and affectionate, drawing on birds, flowers and farm life. Their exchanges are lightly humorous and often reveal character through small misunderstandings, especially Andrew’s initial assumption that Jessamine is the mistress of the house and has a husband.

Characterisation relies on contrast and emblematic traits. Jessamine is gentle, dutiful, uncomplaining and physically diminished by neglect; Andrew is vigorous, observant, practical and kind-hearted. Mrs. John is “stylish,” exacting and querulous, while Aunt Bell embodies immediate maternal welcome. These figures are drawn economically rather than with layered moral ambiguity. Physical appearance reflects inward condition: Jessamine’s pallor and thinness signify emotional starvation, while her sparkling eyes, curling hair and flushed cheeks at Cloverside show recovery. Andrew’s sunburned face, blue eyes and honeysuckle identify him from the outset with health, openness and the country.

The plot is linear and neatly patterned. A chance substitution brings Andrew to the door; repeated floral gifts establish trust; the excursion to Cloverside reveals the possibility of a better life; his temporary absence creates a brief emotional dip; and the threat of Jessamine’s departure precipitates the proposal. Repetition gives the story cohesion, especially the recurring visits, bouquets and doorway encounters. Pacing is brisk, with background exposition compressed into summary and key emotional scenes rendered through dialogue and scenic detail. Transitions such as “The next day,” “After that,” and “One day” reinforce the straightforward, storybook progression.

The dominant motifs are flowers, birds, homes and enclosure. Jessamine is repeatedly imagined as a flower wilting indoors, a “country rose,” or a lark trapped in a cage. Cloverside Farm represents not merely marriage but belonging, freedom and restored identity. The romance therefore grows out of recognition: Andrew sees Jessamine’s unmet needs and offers the home and care denied by her family. The ending is deliberately conclusive—“And she never was”—using the cadence of a fairy-tale assurance to seal the story’s ideal of love as rescue, nurture and permanent domestic happiness.

### Jessamine of Cloverside

When the old Stacy place was sold, Jessamine Stacy felt as though the very earth had been taken from beneath her feet.

It was not a grand home. Its roof sagged over the eastern chamber, the well-chain creaked, and the orchard yielded more moss than apples. But sweet-brier roses climbed about the kitchen window, robins nested in the maples, and beyond the pasture the hills lay purple under the evening sky. Jessamine had been born there, and there she had cared for her father and mother until both were gone.

Her brother John had long since removed to the city. When the farm was lost through debt, he wrote that Jessamine must come to live with him.

“You will be comfortable here,” he said. “And Clara will be glad of your company.”

Clara—Mrs. John Stacy—was stylish, brisk, and never glad of anything that did not save her expense or increase her importance.

At first she told callers that dear Jessamine had come to make her home with them. Before a month had passed, Jessamine was rising before six to light the kitchen fire, dressing the children, washing dishes, mending stockings, carrying coal, answering the bell, and helping the hired girl, when there was one. Presently Clara dismissed the girl altogether.

“It is foolish to keep a servant when there are two women in the house,” she said.

There were two women, certainly; but one made calls and wore pale gloves, while the other baked, scrubbed, swept, and went up and down three flights of stairs until her feet ached at night.

John noticed little. He was worried about business and came home tired.

“You know Clara has a great deal to manage,” he told Jessamine. “Be patient with her.”

Jessamine was patient. She had always been patient. Yet patience could not make the city streets green, nor turn the smoke-darkened sky blue, nor give the hot, stifling kitchen the fragrance of clover.

She grew thin. The roses faded from her cheeks, and her brown hair, once curling and bright, was twisted back without care. Sometimes, while paring potatoes beside the narrow window, she remembered the old orchard after rain so vividly that tears dropped upon her hands.

No one saw them.

One July morning the vegetable wagon stopped at the basement door. Old Mr. Bell, who usually drove it, had broken his leg, and his nephew Andrew was taking the route for a spell.

Andrew Bell was a broad-shouldered young man with a sunburned face, merry blue eyes, and a sprig of honeysuckle caught in his buttonhole. He came down the steps carrying a basket of peas.

“Fine morning,” he said.

Jessamine looked beyond him at the strip of smoky sky.

“Is it?” she asked softly. “I had not noticed.”

Andrew glanced at her more closely. She was pale enough to have been ill, but her eyes were the clear gray of a woodland brook.

“Fine out our way,” he said. “The sun was coming over the rye when I started, and there was mist along the river. It’ll be warm by noon, though.”

“You live in the country?”

“At Cloverside Farm, twelve miles out. My uncle raises truck for the city, and I help him when I’m not busy with my own acres.”

“Twelve miles,” repeated Jessamine, as if he had said twelve steps from paradise. “Are there woods near?”

“A beech wood back of the north meadow, and maples by the house. There’s a brook too, if you don’t mind getting your shoes muddy.”

Jessamine smiled. It changed her face so wonderfully that Andrew forgot the price of the peas.

“Clara!” called a sharp voice from above. “Jessamine, why are you keeping that man?”

The smile vanished.

“I must go,” she said. “How much are the peas?”

On the following morning Andrew brought beans, lettuce, and a bunch of buttercups.

“These aren’t in the bill,” he said, laying the flowers on the table.

Jessamine touched them as though they were gold.

“Did they grow at Cloverside?”

“Right by the lane. Common enough things.”

“They are not common here.”

The next day there were ferns, cool and green from the woods. After that came sweet-brier roses, and then a little sheaf of daisies mixed with red clover. Andrew discovered that he could always find some reason for carrying the basket down himself, though the Bell wagon had served the Stacys for years without such ceremony.

Mrs. John saw the flowers and frowned.

“The vegetable man is becoming very familiar.”

“He is kind,” said Jessamine.

“Kind? I hope you do not encourage him. People in our position must be careful.”

Jessamine looked around the kitchen—the blackened stove, the cracked sink, the heap of children’s aprons waiting to be ironed—and wondered what position Clara meant.

Andrew, meanwhile, was troubled by a misunderstanding.

One morning he said, “Does your husband like the city as well as you do?”

“My husband?” Jessamine stared at him.

“I reckoned you were Mrs. Stacy.”

“No. John is my brother.”

Andrew’s blue eyes brightened.

“Then you aren’t married?”

“No.”

“And this is your brother’s house?”

“Yes.”

“That explains it,” he said.

“What does it explain?”

He reddened under his tan. “Why you didn’t seem like the mistress.”

Jessamine laughed, though there was a little pain in it.

“I am useful here. That is almost the same thing, perhaps.”

It was not the same thing at all, and Andrew knew it. As he drove away, he thought of her in that dim kitchen.

“She’s like a lark shut in a cupboard,” he said aloud. “No wonder she’s forgotten how to sing.”

A week later he asked whether she might go for a drive on Saturday afternoon.

“To Cloverside,” he added hastily. “Aunt Bell wants to meet you. We’ll be back before dark.”

Jessamine’s heart leaped; then it sank.

“Clara will never spare me.”

But Clara was expecting guests and had no wish to explain Jessamine’s worn dress or uncertain place in the household.

“You may go if dinner is finished first,” she said. “And be sure you are back in time to put the children to bed.”

Jessamine worked with such happy speed that even Clara found no fault. At two o’clock Andrew drove up in a clean green wagon behind a stout bay mare. He had brought a broad straw hat for Jessamine.

“The sun is friendly,” he said, “but it can be overfriendly.”

As the streets fell behind them, Jessamine sat very still. Warehouses gave way to scattered houses, houses to gardens, and gardens to open fields. The air changed. It came fresh across the grass, carrying the smell of warm earth and pine woods.

“Oh,” she breathed when the first wide meadow opened before them.

Andrew pretended to attend to the mare, but he saw the colour awakening in her cheeks.

At Cloverside, Aunt Bell came hurrying from the porch—a round, motherly woman with silver spectacles and flour on one arm.

“So this is Jessamine! Andrew has talked of nobody else these three weeks.”

“Aunt!” protested Andrew.

“Well, you haven’t. Come in, child. No—don’t come in yet. You look as if you had been starved for outdoors.”

The farmhouse stood among maples, with honeysuckle over the porch and hollyhocks beside the path. Chickens scratched under the lilacs. Beyond the barn rolled fields of clover, corn, and yellowing grain, and far away the hills rested beneath a blue sky full of shining clouds.

Jessamine wandered from garden to orchard and from orchard to brook. She knelt to dip her fingers in the clear water. She gathered ferns in the beech wood and laughed when Andrew shook a low branch and showered her with leaves.

At supper she drank rich milk and ate Aunt Bell’s brown bread, honey, and raspberry preserves. Aunt Bell watched her with satisfaction.

“You need feeding up,” she declared. “A country girl has no business looking like a white moth.”

“I used to be strong,” said Jessamine. “At home I milked two cows and tended the garden.”

“Did you, now?” Andrew asked. “Can you make butter?”

“Better than you can, I daresay.”

“I can make it come, but Aunt says I pound instead of churn.”

“He does,” said Aunt Bell. “The butter is frightened into gathering.”

Jessamine laughed until her eyes sparkled. Her hair had curled in the country air, and the wind had blown a wild rose colour into her face. Andrew looked at her across the table and thought she belonged there as naturally as the honeysuckle belonged to the porch.

Why should he take her back? Why could he not see her at that table every evening, hear her step in the dairy, and find her flowers in the blue pitcher?

By the time he drove her home, he knew.

At the city door Jessamine’s joy faded a little.

“It has been the happiest day I have had since leaving home,” she said. “Thank you, Andrew.”

“I reckon Cloverside was glad to have you.”

“Places cannot be glad.”

“Can’t they? The house looked brighter to me.”

Before she could answer, Clara called impatiently from above.

Old Mr. Bell recovered soon afterward and resumed the route. Andrew was needed at Cloverside, for harvest had begun, and there were days when every sound hand must work from dawn until the moon rose.

For several weeks Jessamine saw no more of him.

She missed his hearty voice, the sunshine of his blue eyes, and the posies laid carelessly beside the vegetables. Old Mr. Bell brought excellent cabbages but no buttercups. The kitchen seemed darker than before because she had once escaped it.

Then misfortune came to John. His business, which had long been failing, collapsed altogether. Bills appeared; furniture was sold; and Clara alternated between reproaches and tears. John found a position in a western town and announced that they must leave within ten days.

“You will come, of course,” he told Jessamine. “We shall need you more than ever until we are settled.”

The West! To Jessamine it sounded like another city kitchen, only farther from every field she had ever loved.

“But John,” she ventured, “perhaps I could find some other place.”

“What place?” demanded Clara. “You have no money. And after all we have done for you!”

Jessamine said no more.

Old Mr. Bell heard of the failure when he delivered the potatoes. That evening, as Andrew came in from binding the last load of oats, his uncle said, “The Stacys are going west.”

Andrew dropped his hat.

“When?”

“Next Thursday.”

“And Miss Jessamine?”

“Going with them, I suppose.”

Andrew did not wait for supper. He washed at the pump, changed his coat, harnessed the bay mare, and drove toward the city while Aunt Bell stood on the porch smiling to herself.

It was nearly dusk when Jessamine answered the basement bell. At sight of Andrew, her whole tired face brightened.

“You have come back!”

“I came as soon as I heard. Are you going west?”

“I must.”

“No,” said Andrew. “You mustn’t.”

Clara’s voice sounded overhead, but Andrew stepped into the kitchen and shut the door.

“Jessamine, I meant to wait until harvest was over and I had time to say this properly. But there’s no time now, so I’ll say it any way I can.”

She stood with one hand against the table.

“I’ve got a good farm,” he continued, “not grand, but sound. There’s the house under the maples, and Aunt Bell will stay as long as we need her. There are cows to milk, butter to churn, flowers to tend, and a fellow who loves you more every day he lives.”

Jessamine’s lips parted, but no words came.

“I want you at Cloverside,” Andrew said. “Not as somebody useful. Not to wear yourself out for people who never look to see if you’re weary. I want you as my wife, and I’ll do my best to make you happy. Will you come?”

No one had asked what she wanted since her mother died. No one had thought her happiness worth planning for. The wonder of it filled her eyes with tears.

“Oh, Andrew,” she whispered, “do you truly care so much?”

“I reckon I do. More than all the clover fields from here to the hills.”

That was not a fine speech, perhaps, but Jessamine understood it.

“Yes,” she said.

Mrs. John was resentful. She spoke of ingratitude, haste, and social differences; but John, ashamed at last, gave his consent. They were married quietly three days before the family went west.

When Andrew drove his bride to Cloverside, Aunt Bell waited beneath the honeysuckle, and the late roses nodded along the path. The maples were touched with gold, the barns stood full, and cattle moved peacefully home through the fragrant dusk.

Jessamine lifted her face to the open sky.

“You will never be homesick here,” Andrew told her.

And she never was.

The Clockmaker of Bellweather Street

Every clock in Bellweather stopped at 3:17 on the morning that Elias Vale disappeared.

Pocket watches froze in waistcoat pockets. Grandfather clocks held their brass pendulums to one side. The clock above the railway station locked its hands together as if frightened, and the little painted rooster inside Mrs. Finch’s kitchen cuckoo clock leaned halfway through its door without making a sound.

At precisely 3:18, they all began again.

Most people slept through it. Those who noticed blamed the storm, though there had been no lightning, only rain falling in soft, steady sheets over the roofs.

By breakfast, Elias’s daughter Mara found his bed untouched.

His spectacles rested beside a cold cup of tea in the workshop downstairs. His coat remained on its hook. His shoes stood neatly under the bench. In the center of the room, among the springs, gears, pliers, and open-backed watches, lay a single brass key.

It was warm when Mara picked it up.

Her father had made clocks for as long as she could remember. He repaired wedding watches, church clocks, carriage clocks, kitchen clocks, and once an elaborate silver timepiece that played four different tunes depending on the season. People traveled from distant villages to visit Elias Vale because he could hear what was wrong with a clock before opening its case.

“A clock tells you where it hurts,” he used to say. “You only have to stop talking long enough to listen.”

Mara had never been good at listening. She preferred questions.

Where did minutes go after they passed? Why did happy hours feel short and lonely ones feel endless? If two clocks disagreed, which one was lying? Could a person become lost in time as easily as in a forest?

Elias answered most of her questions patiently. But whenever she asked about the locked blue door at the back of the workshop, he became silent.

“Nothing useful is behind it,” he would say.

This was clearly untrue. Her father never locked away useless things.

Now, with rain whispering against the windows and the warm brass key in her hand, Mara approached the blue door.

The key fit.

Beyond it was a narrow staircase spiraling downward, although the workshop had no cellar. Mara took a lamp from the bench and descended.

The air grew colder with each step. Soon she could no longer hear the rain. She counted one hundred and twelve stairs before they ended at a circular chamber deep beneath the street.

Thousands of clocks covered its stone walls.

Some were smaller than coins. Others were as wide as cartwheels. There were clocks with one hand, clocks with thirteen numbers, clocks that ran backward, and clocks with no faces at all. Their ticking blended into a restless murmur, like a crowd speaking in sleep.

At the center of the chamber stood a black iron clock twice Mara’s height.

It had no hands. In place of a face was a round glass window, behind which gray mist swirled.

A chain ran from the clock to the floor. At its end lay a silver pocket watch.

Mara recognized it immediately. Elias always carried it, though he never used it to tell the hour.

She bent to pick it up.

The moment her fingers touched the silver case, the great black clock struck once.

The sound passed through her bones.

The glass window filled with light, and the mist cleared to reveal not gears, but a street.

Bellweather Street.

It looked almost as it had the day before, except the sky was perfectly white, and the buildings had no shadows. People stood motionless along the pavements: the baker holding a tray, a child reaching for a rolling hoop, the postman with one foot raised above a puddle.

In the distance, a solitary figure walked toward the railway station.

“Father!” Mara shouted.

The figure stopped.

Elias turned. Even through the glass, she saw his expression change from exhaustion to alarm.

He ran toward her.

“Mara, what have you done?”

His voice sounded faint, as if carried down a long tunnel.

“What have I done? Where are you?”

“Between seconds.” He looked over his shoulder. “You must close the clock.”

“How?”

“The key. Turn it to the left.”

Mara reached for the brass key still clutched in her palm, but before she could insert it into the iron clock, something moved behind Elias.

At first she thought it was another person. Then it unfolded.

It was tall and thin, dressed in a coat made from overlapping strips of darkness. Its arms hung below its knees. Where its face should have been, a white clock dial showed only one hand.

That hand pointed at Elias.

He turned and ran.

The creature followed without hurrying. With every step, it crossed half the distance between them.

Mara thrust the key into a slot beneath the glass and turned left.

The clock screamed.

The chamber vanished.

She landed hard on the workshop floor as the blue door slammed behind her. Every clock in the room chimed at once, though the hour was 8:43.

Then the shop became quiet.

Mara pulled at the blue door. It would not open. The brass key had disappeared.

Someone knocked at the front entrance.

It was Constable Reed, dripping rain onto the floor. Behind him stood Mrs. Finch, the baker, and half the street, all talking at once.

They wanted their clocks repaired.

Since 3:17 that morning, the town’s timepieces had developed peculiar faults. Mrs. Finch’s cuckoo clock ran correctly, but the bird announced things that had not yet happened. The station clock lost nine minutes whenever a train approached. The church clock struck according to the number of people praying inside. The baker’s alarm rang whenever his bread was about to burn, even when he had not set it.

Constable Reed placed his pocket watch on the counter.

Its second hand trembled but refused to move forward.

“Where’s your father?” he asked.

Mara looked at the crowd.

“Visiting a client.”

“When will he return?”

“I don’t know.”

A murmur passed through the shop. Bellweather trusted Elias with time the way it trusted Dr. Thorne with illness and Reverend Pike with death. His absence frightened them.

Mara straightened.

“I can repair the clocks.”

It was not entirely a lie. Elias had taught her the basics. She could replace a spring, clean a wheel, reset a pendulum, and identify most common faults. Yet there was nothing common about a cuckoo predicting that the mayor would fall into the fountain at noon.

Which, according to Mrs. Finch, he did.

Mara spent the day examining watches. None was broken. Their gears were clean, their springs sound. Something else disturbed them, something that moved invisibly through the town.

Near sunset, she opened her father’s silver pocket watch.

Inside the lid, scratched into the metal, were four words:

TIME OWES NO ONE.

Beneath the mechanism she found a folded piece of paper covered in Elias’s cramped handwriting.

If the Hourless One wakes, it will follow the oldest stolen hour. Return what was taken before the thirteenth bell. Do not bargain with it.

Mara read the message three times.

Then she heard ticking from behind the blue door.

Not many clocks. One.

Slow.

Patient.

She searched the workshop until midnight, opening cabinets and pulling books from shelves. At last she found her father’s journal hidden inside the case of a broken mantel clock.

The early pages contained repair notes, household accounts, and reminders to buy tea. Halfway through, the handwriting changed. The lines became crowded and urgent.

Twenty years ago, when Mara was an infant, she had fallen ill with scarlet fever.

She knew that much. Elias had told her she had nearly died. He never explained how she recovered.

The journal did.

On the worst night of her illness, the doctor told Elias she would not survive until morning. Desperate, he went beneath the workshop and opened the black clock, an ancient machine built by clockmakers who believed time could be stored, borrowed, and traded.

Elias stole one hour from the clock.

During that hour, Mara’s fever broke.

But stolen time had to come from somewhere. The hour was taken from Bellweather’s future and sealed in a silver watch. Elias believed he could keep it hidden. Instead, the theft awakened the guardian inside the space between seconds.

The Hourless One.

It hunted stolen time and those who carried it.

For twenty years Elias had drawn it away from Mara, entering the black clock whenever it came near. Each time he escaped. This time, he had not returned.

Mara looked at the silver watch in her hand.

She understood then why her father carried it. He had not been keeping time.

He had been carrying her stolen hour.

The workshop’s clocks began to strike one.

Between the first and second chime, a shadow crossed the front window.

Between the second and third, it reached the door.

There was no fourth.

Mara turned.

The Hourless One stood inside the shop.

It had entered without opening the door. Its coat trailed into the dark corners of the room. The single hand on its white face pointed at the silver watch.

Mara could not move.

A voice came from inside the creature, layered from many voices speaking together.

“RETURN.”

She remembered her father’s warning: Do not bargain with it.

So, naturally, she said, “Take me to my father.”

The hand on its face shifted toward her.

“RETURN.”

“I have the hour. You need me.”

The clocks on the shelves began running backward.

The Hourless One extended one long hand.

Mara placed the silver watch in its palm but did not let go.

“My father first.”

For a moment nothing happened.

Then the shop stretched like a reflection on disturbed water. The walls bent away, the ceiling rose into whiteness, and the floor became Bellweather Street.

Mara stood between seconds.

The town was frozen around her. Rain hung in the air like glass beads. In an upper window, a candle flame remained perfectly still. A blackbird hovered above a chimney, wings spread.

The Hourless One released the watch and pointed toward the station.

Mara ran.

She found Elias in the waiting room. He sat against the wall beneath the silent station clock. His hair had gone completely white, though that morning it had still been more brown than gray.

He looked up and laughed once in disbelief.

“You never listen.”

“I listened to your journal.”

“I wrote that you must not bargain with it.”

“I listened selectively.”

Mara helped him stand. He seemed weak, almost weightless.

“How long have you been here?” she asked.

“I don’t know. There are no hours here.”

The Hourless One appeared on the platform.

Its clock-face hand pointed at Mara.

“RETURN.”

Elias stepped in front of her. “Take the watch.”

“It doesn’t want the watch,” Mara said. “Not really.”

She had finally understood the message. The stolen hour was not stored in the silver case. The watch had only hidden its trail.

The hour lived in her.

It was the hour in which her fever had broken, the extra hour her life had been given.

Elias gripped her arm. “No.”

“The hour has to be returned.”

“No.”

“If I don’t return it, that thing will keep coming. The clocks will keep failing. Maybe all of Bellweather will end up trapped here.”

“I will find another way.”

“You had twenty years.”

His face tightened as though she had struck him.

Mara softened her voice. “You gave me more than one hour, Father. You gave me twenty years.”

“And I want twenty more.”

“So do I.”

The Hourless One moved closer.

Around them, the station trembled. Cracks appeared in the white sky. Through them Mara glimpsed darkness filled with turning wheels.

The clock above the platform began to strike.

Once.

Elias pulled the brass key from his pocket. “When it reaches thirteen, the space between seconds will close. If we are inside, we stay inside.”

Twice.

“Then go,” Mara said.

“Not without you.”

Three times.

The Hourless One reached for her.

Mara opened the silver watch. Its hands stood at 3:17.

“Tell me how to return the hour.”

Elias shook his head.

Four.

“Tell me!”

“No father should teach his child how to die.”

“No child should have to watch her father vanish because he is too stubborn to be saved.”

Five.

The creature’s fingers closed around Mara’s wrist. Cold rushed through her. Memories flashed before her eyes: her first morning in the workshop, Elias lifting her so she could see a music box; rain on the windows; burnt toast; birthdays; arguments; quiet evenings spent sorting gears.

She felt the Hourless One searching through her life.

Six.

Elias seized the creature’s arm, but his hands passed through its coat.

“It will take the hour from your beginning,” he said desperately. “Everything after it may disappear.”

“May?”

“I don’t know.”

Seven.

Mara smiled despite her fear. “You always hated not knowing.”

“I still do.”

Eight.

The station walls peeled away. Beyond them stretched an endless white plain crowded with motionless people. Mara realized they were not only from Bellweather. There were thousands from different places and different centuries: soldiers, sailors, children, kings, farmers. People caught between one instant and the next, perhaps all because someone, somewhere, had tried to steal a little more time.

Nine.

The Hourless One raised its other hand toward the watch.

Mara saw the answer.

The silver case had an empty keyhole in its back.

“Give me the key,” she said.

Ten.

Elias closed his fist around it.

“Please,” Mara said.

Eleven.

He placed the key in her palm.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered.

“For saving me?”

“For making the choice for you.”

Mara inserted the key into the watch.

“I’m not.”

Twelve.

She turned it to the right.

The watch sprang open with a burst of golden light.

Warmth poured from Mara’s chest. It did not hurt. That surprised her. She felt the stolen hour rising through her like a remembered song—the cool cloth on her childhood forehead, her father’s hand wrapped around hers, the first deep breath she had taken as the fever released her.

The light entered the silver watch.

The hands began to move.

3:18.

The Hourless One bowed its head.

Then the thirteenth bell rang.

The world shattered.

Mara woke to birdsong.

She lay on the floor of the workshop with one hand still wrapped around the brass key. Sunlight streamed through the windows. The storm had passed.

The blue door was gone. In its place stood a plain wall crowded with clocks.

All of them showed 7:06.

All of them were ticking.

Mara sat up too quickly and nearly fainted. Someone caught her shoulders.

“Careful,” Elias said.

She stared at him.

He looked exhausted, and his hair remained white, but he was alive.

“So am I,” she said.

He laughed and pulled her into his arms.

For several minutes neither spoke. Around them, the clocks continued their steady conversation.

At last Mara noticed the silver watch lying nearby. Its hands moved normally. Inside the lid, the scratched message had changed.

TIME OWES NO ONE, it still read.

Beneath it were two new words.

LIVE ANYWAY.

In the days that followed, Bellweather’s clocks returned to their ordinary habits. Mrs. Finch’s cuckoo stopped predicting accidents. The church bell no longer counted worshippers. The station clock behaved itself, although it always ran one minute slow in heavy rain.

No one remembered Elias disappearing.

No one except Mara and Elias remembered the clocks stopping at 3:17.

There were consequences.

Mara had feared she might lose the twenty years that followed her stolen hour. Instead, she lost pieces of them. Some memories vanished completely. She no longer remembered learning to read or the tune her mother used to sing before her death. She forgot the name of her first friend and the taste of the cake from her tenth birthday.

Other memories remained but changed around the edges, as if they belonged to someone else.

Elias remembered everything for both of them.

When she asked, he told her the stories. Often she corrected details by instinct.

“I would never have climbed onto the church roof,” she said one evening.

“You did.”

“Why?”

“To see whether the weather vane knew which way the wind would turn before it turned.”

“That does sound like me.”

“It does.”

Years passed.

Elias taught Mara every craft he knew. This time she listened—not because she had stopped asking questions, but because she finally understood that listening was another way of asking.

When Elias became too old for delicate work, Mara took over the shop. She repaired watches and clocks from across the country. People said she had inherited her father’s gift. She could hear what was wrong with a clock before opening it.

Sometimes, late at night, she heard another sound beneath the familiar ticking: a single distant bell, ringing from somewhere no map could name.

She never searched for the blue door.

After Elias died at the age of eighty-seven, Mara placed his silver watch in the workshop window. She left it open so passersby could read the words inside.

Many paused to look.

Some understood. Most did not.

On the first anniversary of his death, a young girl entered the shop carrying a broken alarm clock. She had fierce eyebrows, muddy boots, and too many questions.

“Where do minutes go after they pass?” the girl asked while Mara examined the clock.

“I don’t know.”

“Why do happy hours feel short?”

“I don’t know.”

“If two clocks disagree, which one is lying?”

Mara smiled.

“I don’t know.”

The girl frowned. “You’re a clockmaker. Shouldn’t you know about time?”

“My dear,” Mara said, opening the clock’s brass case, “clockmakers know less about time than anyone. We only know how precious it is.”

Outside, Bellweather Street shone after the rain. People hurried beneath umbrellas, complaining of delays, wasting minutes, saving seconds, promising tomorrow, remembering yesterday.

Above them, the railway clock moved from 3:17 to 3:18.

No shadows unfolded.

No doors appeared.

The next minute arrived freely, belonging to no one until it was lived.
